historical_timeline.summary: Her head tremor was noticeable in a television film.
Starred in On Golden Pond, which brought her fourth Academy Award.
In a documentary, said she had inherited her shaking head from her grandfather.
Died at her home in Old Saybrook, Connecticut, at 96.

claims.statement: Katharine Hepburn was born in Hartford, Connecticut, on May 12, 1907.
Hepburn died on June 29, 2003, at her home in Old Saybrook, Connecticut, at 96. The executor of her estate said she had been in declining health in recent years and died of old age.
claims.clinical_interpretation: Record the death as a fact without detail.

claims.statement: By the 1980s Hepburn had a noticeable tremor that left her head constantly shaking; it was noticeable by the time of a 1979 television film and worsened later in her life.
claims.clinical_interpretation: The anchor for the synthetic head tremor; the visible tremor fixes the index year.

claims.statement: Hepburn spoke publicly about the tremor. In a 1993 documentary she said that she had inherited her shaking head from her grandfather Hepburn, and she denied the common belief that she had Parkinson's disease. A magazine editor who interviewed her recalled that she called it a familial tremor inherited from her grandfather.
claims.clinical_interpretation: Her own public account; it anchors the synthetic family history and supports essential tremor over Parkinson's disease.

claims.statement: An obituary described her famous voice in her last years as quivery.
claims.clinical_interpretation: Public description that anchors the synthetic voice tremor; it describes a later period than the episode.

claims.statement: Her tremor is identified as essential tremor by an encyclopedia article, a public radio report, and a physician's newspaper column, all of which note that it was widely mistaken for Parkinson's disease; an Associated Press obituary described tremors similar to Parkinson's disease. No public statement by a physician who examined her was found.
claims.clinical_interpretation: The diagnostic label is a retrospective interpretation; the modern record codes essential tremor with verification provisional.

claims.statement: Hepburn won a fourth Academy Award for Best Actress for On Golden Pond (1981) and published her autobiography, Me: Stories of My Life, in 1991.
claims.clinical_interpretation: Context only; both postdate the episode.

synthetic_episode.teaching_objective: Evaluation and treatment of essential tremor in a 72-year-old woman with a visible head tremor, a mild voice tremor, and action tremor of both hands: diagnosis by the MDS consensus classification and distinction from Parkinson's disease, exclusion of thyroid and drug causes, a standard tremor rating with spiral drawing and handwriting at every visit, propranolol with heart rate, blood pressure, asthma, mood, fatigue, and fall checks, primidone as the alternative with its sedation and fall risks at her age, voice therapy, occupational therapy for adaptive aids, botulinum toxin for head and voice tremor, and the criteria for referral for focused ultrasound or deep brain stimulation, on the AAN essential tremor guidelines with CMID general items for older adults. The Parkinson's disease label that some accounts gave her tremor is recorded as a contested retrospective interpretation, not a diagnosis.

documentation.chief_complaint: Four-week tremor follow-up, seen the same day by movement disorders neurology

hpi.narrative: Ms. Hepburn is a 72-year-old woman with a shaky hand she has noticed for several years and a head tremor that has been visible for at least a year and has slowly worsened, who returns four weeks after her first visit and is seen by movement disorders neurology on the same day. She notices the hand tremor most when carrying a full cup, pouring, writing letters, and signing her name; she now carries cups half full. The head tremor bothers others more than her, and she finds it settles when she rests her head against a high-backed chair. Her voice wavers on sustained notes on stage. She has had no stiffness, slowness, shuffling, falls, numbness, or change in memory. She takes no medicines and has one cup of coffee in the morning. She says her grandfather's head and hand shook too, and she wants it known that this is not Parkinson's disease. Her thyroid test and blood tests from the first visit were normal.

assessment_plan.assessment: Neurology finds the picture typical of essential tremor by the MDS consensus classification: bilateral upper-limb action tremor present for more than three years with head and voice tremor and no other neurological signs, and nothing to suggest Parkinson's disease or dystonia. Thyroid and metabolic causes are excluded, and she takes no drug that worsens tremor. The hand tremor interferes with daily tasks and her work, so treatment is reasonable. She has no asthma, slow pulse, heart block, or diabetes, so propranolol is suitable

hpi.narrative: Ms. Hepburn returns three months after her first visit and twelve weeks after starting propranolol extended-release 60 mg each morning. Her hands are steadier: she can carry a full cup again and signs letters more easily, though writing still tires her hand. The head tremor is about the same. She finished the six-week voice therapy course a month ago and uses breath support and a slightly higher pitch on stage, which steadies sustained notes. She has had no lightheadedness on standing, wheeze, cold hands, unusual tiredness, vivid dreams, or low mood, and no falls. Occupational therapy has not yet been booked.

hpi.narrative: Ms. Hepburn is a 73-year-old woman with essential tremor of the head, voice, and hands who returns for her subsequent annual wellness visit, two months after her six-month tremor review. She completed the health risk assessment before the visit. She takes propranolol extended-release 60 mg each morning and has missed no doses. Her hands are steadier with cups and pens, and since the occupational therapy visit seven weeks ago she uses weighted utensils, a lidded travel cup, and a thicker pen. The head tremor is unchanged and does not trouble her. She uses the breath-support techniques from voice therapy on stage. She has had no falls, emergency visits, or hospital stays this year, and no lightheadedness, wheezing, or low mood. She swims and walks most days.

referral.question: Head, voice, and bilateral hand tremor in a 72-year-old woman, the hand tremor present for several years and the head tremor visible for at least a year and slowly worsening, which others have taken for Parkinson's disease. Please confirm the diagnosis, advise on treatment for the hand tremor that interferes with her daily tasks and stage work, and advise on the head and voice tremor
referral.urgency: Routine, within four weeks, on the same day as her four-week primary care check
referral.pertinent_history: Side-to-side head tremor visible for at least a year and slowly worse; postural and kinetic tremor of both hands for several years, right slightly more than left, with spilling and shaky handwriting; wavering pitch on sustained vowels. She reports that her grandfather's head and hand shook. No stiffness, slowness, imbalance, falls, or memory change. Today: TETRAS performance subscale 22 of 64 and daily-living subscale 14 of 48; spiral drawing with tremor waves; no rest tremor, bradykinesia, rigidity, dystonic posturing, or ataxia; tandem gait normal; Timed Up and Go 9 seconds. TSH 2.2, blood count, and basic chemistry normal. MoCA 28 of 30 and PHQ-9 2. Pulse 78 and blood pressure 132/78 mmHg; no asthma, heart block, or diabetes. No medicines; one cup of coffee daily
questions: Does she meet the MDS consensus criteria for essential tremor, and is there anything to suggest Parkinson's disease, dystonic tremor, or essential tremor plus that would call for imaging?
Which medicine do you recommend first, propranolol or primidone, at her age, and with what monitoring?
What can be offered for the head tremor and the voice tremor?
What rehabilitation or aids would help with eating, drinking, and writing?
At what point would focused ultrasound thalamotomy or deep brain stimulation be considered?
How often should she be followed, and by whom?

consultant_note.history: Ms. Hepburn, a 72-year-old actress, is seen at the request of Dr. Price for a tremor of the head, voice, and hands. The head tremor has been visible for at least a year and has slowly worsened; it is side to side and settles when she rests her head against a high-backed chair. Her hands have shaken for several years when she carries a full cup, pours, writes, and signs her name, and she now carries cups half full. Her voice wavers on sustained notes on stage. She has no tremor of the hands at rest, no stiffness, slowness, shuffling, falls, numbness, or memory change. She takes no medicines, drinks one cup of coffee in the morning, and has no asthma. She says her grandfather's head and hand shook as well
consultant_note.data_reviewed: Dr. Price's first-visit assessment four weeks ago: TETRAS performance and daily-living subscales, spiral drawing, Timed Up and Go, MoCA 28, and PHQ-9 2; TSH, blood count, and basic chemistry from the same visit, all normal; and today's pulse and seated and standing blood pressure

exam.finding: Alert, direct, and engaged; normal facial expression and blink rate
Side-to-side head tremor of moderate amplitude, less when the head is supported, with no head tilt, turning, or null point; wavering pitch on a sustained vowel
Postural and kinetic tremor of both hands, right slightly more than left, without intention increase near the target; no tremor at rest; no dystonic posturing of the hands
Normal tone; no bradykinesia or decrement on finger and foot tapping
Finger-to-nose accurate apart from the tremor; tandem gait normal; normal arm swing; no freezing
TETRAS performance subscale 22 of 64; spiral drawing with tremor waves in both hands
Pulse 76 and regular; 130/76 mmHg seated and 128/76 mmHg standing

assessment.assessment: Essential tremor by the MDS consensus classification: an isolated action tremor of both upper limbs for more than three years, with head and voice tremor and no other neurological signs. There is no rest tremor, bradykinesia, or rigidity to suggest Parkinson's disease; no abnormal posture, head turning, or null point to suggest dystonic tremor; and no tandem-gait, memory, or other soft signs that would make it essential tremor plus. The reported family history fits. A dopamine transporter scan or brain MRI would add nothing

Propranolol and primidone are both established first-line treatments for limb tremor. At 72 she has no asthma, slow pulse, heart block, or diabetes, so propranolol is suitable and avoids the sedation, unsteadiness, and fall risk primidone carries at her age. The extended-release form allows one morning dose

Head and voice tremor respond less to medicines than hand tremor. Propranolol may help the head tremor. Botulinum toxin injection is an option for a disabling head or voice tremor, but neither is disabling now, and voice therapy techniques can steady her sustained notes
Focused ultrasound thalamotomy and deep brain stimulation are for disabling limb tremor that persists after adequate trials of propranolol and primidone. They are not indicated now

recommendations: Start propranolol extended-release 60 mg each morning; do not stop it suddenly
Check resting pulse and seated and 3-minute standing blood pressure at each visit on propranolol, and ask about wheeze, fatigue, low mood, and lightheadedness; repeat the PHQ-9 after three months

If the hand tremor still limits her after a fair trial, raise propranolol as the pulse allows, or add primidone at 12.5 to 25 mg at bedtime, increased slowly, with checks for sedation and unsteadiness
Speech-language therapy for the voice tremor
Occupational therapy for adaptive aids: weighted utensils, a lidded cup, and a thick-barreled pen
Botulinum toxin injection for the head or voice tremor if either becomes disabling
No brain imaging or dopamine transporter scan
Keep caffeine modest, and review any new medicine for tremor-worsening effects
Refer for focused ultrasound thalamotomy or deep brain stimulation only if disabling limb tremor persists after adequate trials of propranolol and primidone
Primary care follows her every three to six months with TETRAS, spiral drawing, pulse, standing blood pressure, side effects, and falls
consultant_note.communication: Discussed with Dr. Price, who sees her the same day. The diagnosis and plan were explained to Ms. Hepburn, who was glad to hear plainly that this is not Parkinson's disease and agreed to the plan
consultant_note.follow_up: Movement disorders review in one year, or sooner if the tremor worsens, propranolol is not tolerated, or any sign beyond tremor appears
